text: Teleportation sends 1 qubit of quantum information using 2 classical bits and 1 shared entangled qubit. Superdense coding runs that resource trade in reverse: it sends 2 classical bits using only 1 transmitted qubit, by spending 1 shared entangled qubit to make it possible.

Alice and Bob pre-share a Bell pair, Phi-plus, one qubit each. Alice wants to send a 2-bit classical message but is only allowed to physically transmit one qubit. Without entanglement, that's simply impossible — a well-established result called the Holevo bound says a single unentangled qubit carries at most 1 classical bit when measured. Pre-shared entanglement is what changes the arithmetic.

Depending on the message, Alice applies one of four operations to her own qubit only — she never touches Bob's. Sending 00 means doing nothing, leaving Phi-plus unchanged. Sending 01 means applying X, giving Psi-plus. Sending 10 means applying Z, giving Phi-minus. Sending 11 means applying Z then X, giving the fourth Bell state. These four results are exactly the four Bell states, and critically, they're mutually orthogonal — each perfectly distinguishable from the other three.

Alice sends her one qubit to Bob, who now holds both qubits and performs a single Bell-basis measurement. Because the four possible results are mutually orthogonal, this identifies with certainty which operation Alice applied, recovering the full 2 bits from the one qubit transmitted. If the four states had overlapped instead, the measurement would sometimes be ambiguous — the same mismatched-basis problem from chapter 3. Here, by construction, there's no ambiguity at all.

Lay the two protocols side by side: teleportation sends 1 qubit of quantum information using 2 classical bits plus 1 shared pair; superdense coding sends 2 classical bits using 1 transmitted qubit plus that same 1 shared pair. Both consume exactly one pre-shared entangled pair as fuel, and neither works without it — remove the entanglement, and superdense coding is capped at the ordinary classical limit of 1 bit per qubit.
